question:
Choose the best substitute for the bracketed segment in the following sentence to complete the sentence meaningfully.
(No sooner did she shouted), than the thieves ran away leaving all the jewellery on the table.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No sooner did she shout.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence uses the structure "No sooner...than", which is used to describe two actions that happened in very quick succession — as soon as the first action took place, the second one followed immediately.

• Rule — No sooner...than:
◦ No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + subject + V2 (Past Perfect construction)
◦ No sooner + did + subject + V1 + than + subject + V2 (Simple Past with "did" construction)

• In the bracketed segment, "did" is already used, so the verb that follows must be in its base form (V1), i.e. "shout", not the past form "shouted". Using both "did" and "shouted" together is a case of double marking of tense, which is grammatically incorrect.

• Applying the rule: No sooner did she shout, than the thieves ran away...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No sooner do she shouts" is incorrect because the auxiliary "do" does not agree with the third person singular subject "she" (it should be "does"), and even then the base verb "shout", not "shouts", must follow.

• Option 2: "No sooner does she shout" is incorrect because "No sooner" must be followed by a past structure (with "did" or "had"), not the simple present auxiliary "does", since the action being described is a completed past event.

• Option 3: "No sooner had she shout" is incorrect because after the auxiliary "had", the verb must be in its past participle (V3) form, i.e. "shouted", not the base form "shout".

NOTE

• Similar inversion structures frequently asked in SSC exams: "Hardly/Scarcely...when", "Not only...but also", "Never...had" — all of these use inverted auxiliary-subject order when placed at the start of the sentence.

• Remember: after "did" always use V1 (base form); after "had" always use V3 (past participle).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Mathematical problems are never solved daily by him.
option_1: He never solves mathematical problems daily.
option_2: He has solved never mathematical problems daily.
option_3: He solve never mathematical problems daily.
option_4: He solves never mathematical problems daily.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He never solves mathematical problems daily.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Mathematical problems are never solved daily by him" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Present Tense, with the negative adverb "never" placed between the auxiliary and the main verb.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + (never) + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + does/do + not/never + V1 + Object (with "never" placed before the main verb, after the subject)

• Applying the rule: the agent "him" becomes the subject "He"; since the subject is third person singular, the verb takes "-s", giving "solves"; the adverb "never" is placed immediately before the verb; and the passive subject "Mathematical problems" becomes the object.

• Active form: He never solves mathematical problems daily.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has solved never" wrongly uses the Present Perfect auxiliary "has", which does not correspond to the Simple Present passive of the original sentence, and also places "never" after the verb, which is ungrammatical.

• Option 3 is incorrect because the verb "solve" does not agree with the third person singular subject "He" — it must take the "-s" ending, i.e. "solves".

• Option 4 is incorrect because the word order "solves never" is wrong; the adverb "never" must come before the main verb, not after it, in a simple tense active sentence.

NOTE

• Adverbs of frequency such as "never", "always", "often", "usually", "sometimes" are placed before the main verb but after the auxiliary/"to be" verb in a sentence — e.g. "He is never late" but "He never comes late."

• When converting passive to active with a frequency adverb, always keep the adverb in its normal mid-position in the active sentence, i.e. before the main verb.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
My colleages have lacked the conscience needed to be morally correct on this grave issue.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. colleages.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "colleages" is misspelt in the given sentence. The correct spelling is "colleagues" — a person one works with, especially in a profession.

• Spelling key: COLL + EAGUE + S. Note the "gue" ending (as in "league", "vague", "rogue"), which is missing in the incorrect form "colleages".

• The rest of the sentence — "have lacked the conscience needed to be morally correct on this grave issue" — is grammatically and orthographically correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "conscience" is spelt correctly and used correctly — it means the inner sense of right and wrong.

• Option 3: "morally" is spelt correctly — the adverb form of "moral", meaning in a manner concerned with right conduct.

• Option 4: "grave" is spelt correctly and used correctly in the sense of "serious".

NOTE

• Commonly confused/misspelt "-gue" ending words in SSC exams: colleague, league, vague, rogue, fatigue, intrigue, catalogue, dialogue.

• Do not confuse "conscience" (moral sense of right/wrong) with "conscious" (aware) — these are frequently tested together in SSC vocabulary/spelling questions.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
When Mayank came, / I shall go / with him to / the circus.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. When Mayank came.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a future action — "I shall go with him to the circus" — that is dependent on the time clause "When Mayank came".

• Rule — Time clauses referring to a future event: when a sentence describes something that will happen in the future, the clause beginning with time conjunctions such as "when", "till", "until", "before", "after", "as soon as" must use the Simple Present Tense, even though the overall sense is future — never the Simple Past or a future form.

• Since the main clause "I shall go with him to the circus" is in the future, the time clause must also be future in sense, so "came" (Simple Past) is wrong and should be changed to "comes" (Simple Present).

• Corrected sentence: "When Mayank comes, I shall go with him to the circus."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "with him to" is correct — the preposition "to" correctly indicates destination, and "with him" correctly shows accompaniment.

• Option 3: "I shall go" is correct as it stands — "shall" is used correctly with the first person subject "I" to express a simple future action.

• Option 4: "the circus" is correct — a simple noun phrase acting as the object of the preposition "to", with no error.

NOTE

• This rule is often called the rule of "Future in the subordinate clause of time and condition": such clauses (starting with if, when, unless, till, until, before, after, as soon as) never take "will/shall"; they use the Simple Present even for future reference.

• Example: "I will call you when he arrives" (not "will arrive"); "She will start the project as soon as she gets approval" (not "will get").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Bite the bullet
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To endure a painful situation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bite the bullet" means to face or endure a painful, difficult, or unpleasant situation with courage because it is unavoidable. (कठिन परिस्थिति को साहसपूर्वक सहना)
◦ Example: With no other option left, he decided to bite the bullet and accept the pay cut.

• The idiom is believed to have originated from the practice of having wounded soldiers bite on a bullet (or a piece of leather/wood) to help them cope with pain during surgery before anaesthesia was available.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To take a risk (जोखिम उठाना): matches the idiom "To bell the cat" or "To take the plunge", not "bite the bullet".

• Option 2: To enjoy something immensely (अत्यधिक आनंद लेना): matches idioms like "To have a whale of a time", not "bite the bullet".

• Option 4: To criticise someone harshly (कड़ी आलोचना करना): matches idioms like "To pull someone to pieces" or "To rake someone over the coals", not "bite the bullet".

NOTE

• Other idioms about enduring hardship often asked in SSC: "To grin and bear it" (to endure something unpleasant without complaint), "To weather the storm" (to survive a difficult period), and "To face the music" (to accept the unpleasant consequences of one's actions).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Awkward
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Graceful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Awkward" means clumsy, lacking skill or grace, or causing embarrassment. (भद्दा/अनाड़ी)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Graceful", meaning having elegance or beauty of movement, form, or manner. (सुंदर/सुडौल)
◦ Example: Despite her nervousness, the dancer moved with a graceful ease on stage, quite unlike her usual awkward manner.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Meaningful" (अर्थपूर्ण) is the opposite of "meaningless", not of "awkward".

• Option 3: "Innocent" (निर्दोष) is the opposite of "guilty", not of "awkward".

• Option 4: "Huge" (विशाल) is the opposite of "tiny/small", not of "awkward".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Awkward": clumsy, gauche, ungainly, ungraceful, uncoordinated.

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested with "graceful": graceful ↔ clumsy, graceful ↔ inelegant.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
On the day of independence, a jubilant crowd from all over the country cheered and wept.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Gloomy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Jubilant" means feeling or expressing great happiness and triumph; extremely joyful. (हर्षित/उल्लासित)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Gloomy", meaning dark, depressing, or feeling sad and without hope. (उदास/निराश)
◦ Example: The jubilant celebrations of the winning team stood in sharp contrast to the gloomy silence of the losing side.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Triumphant" (विजयी) is a synonym of "jubilant", not its antonym — it means feeling great satisfaction from success.

• Option 2: "Cryptic" (रहस्यमय) means mysterious or puzzling in meaning; it is unrelated to the emotion expressed by "jubilant".

• Option 3: "Elated" (उत्साहित) is also a synonym of "jubilant", meaning very happy and excited.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Jubilant": elated, triumphant, exultant, overjoyed, ecstatic.

• Other antonym pairs with "gloomy": gloomy ↔ cheerful, gloomy ↔ radiant, gloomy ↔ jubilant.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
It is raining a lot in April and May, but the summer is very dry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. rains a lot in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a general, habitual truth about the weather in the months of April and May — a recurring pattern, not an action happening right now.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense: the Simple Present Tense (Subject + V1/V5) is used to express habitual actions, general truths, and permanent facts, whereas the Present Continuous Tense ("is/am/are + V-ing") is used only for actions happening at the moment of speaking or for temporary/planned situations.

• Since "raining a lot in April and May" is a recurring seasonal fact (further confirmed by the contrast with "but the summer is very dry", also in the Simple Present), the verb must be in the Simple Present: "rains", with the subject "It" taking the third-person singular "-s" form, followed by the correct preposition "in" (used with months).

• Corrected sentence: "It rains a lot in April and May, but the summer is very dry."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was raining a lot on" is incorrect — it wrongly uses the Past Continuous tense and the wrong preposition "on" (used with dates/days, not months).

• Option 2: "will rains a lot of" is incorrect — after the modal "will", the base form "rain" (not "rains") must be used, and "of" is the wrong preposition here.

• Option 4: "rain a lot at" is incorrect — the subject "It" is third person singular, so the verb must take "-s" ("rains"), and the preposition "at" is used with specific points/times, not months.

NOTE

• Prepositions of time: "in" is used with months, years and seasons (in April, in 2023, in summer); "on" is used with days and dates (on Monday, on 5th May); "at" is used with precise clock times (at 5 o'clock).

• The Simple Present is also used for scheduled/timetabled future events, e.g. "The train leaves at 6 pm."

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who conforms to accepted behaviour or established practices.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Conformist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Conformist" is a person who conforms to accepted behaviour or established practices; one who follows conventions or general opinion without questioning. (परंपरावादी/यथास्थितिवादी)
◦ Example: As a strict conformist, he never challenged the office dress code, however outdated it seemed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Psychologist" (मनोवैज्ञानिक) means a person who studies the human mind and behaviour scientifically — unrelated to conforming to norms.

• Option 3: "Socialist" (समाजवादी) means a person who believes in socialism, a political and economic system based on collective ownership.

• Option 4: "Rebelist" is not a standard English word; the correct related word is "Rebel", meaning a person who resists authority or established convention — in fact the opposite of a conformist.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often confused in SSC exams: Nonconformist (one who does NOT conform to accepted behaviour — opposite of "Conformist"), Maverick (an unconventional/independent-minded person), Iconoclast (one who attacks cherished beliefs/traditions).

• Word-building tip: the prefix "non-" reverses meaning — Conformist ↔ Nonconformist.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
The fields remained barren despite the efforts of the local administration and agricultural scientists.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Fertile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Barren" means (of land) too poor to produce much or any vegetation; unable to bear crops or offspring. (बंजर/अनुपजाऊ)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Fertile", meaning (of land) able to produce a large amount of good-quality crops or vegetation; productive. (उपजाऊ)
◦ Example: Years of irrigation projects finally turned the once-barren land into a fertile plain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sterile" (बंजर/निष्फल) is actually a synonym of "barren", not its antonym — it also means unable to produce crops or offspring.

• Option 2: "Unforgiving" (क्षमा न करने वाला) means not willing to forgive, or (of a situation) leaving no room for error — unrelated to land productivity.

• Option 3: "Damp" (नम) means slightly wet; it describes moisture, not the productivity of land, and damp land is not necessarily fertile.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Barren": sterile, infertile, unproductive, arid, desolate.

• Other antonym pairs with "fertile": fertile ↔ barren, fertile ↔ sterile, fertile ↔ arid.

question:
Identity the correct spelling of the underlined word.
It is considered a great phenamina in the field of economics.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. phenomena.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "phenomena" — the plural of "phenomenon", referring to a fact, occurrence, or circumstance that is observed to exist, especially one whose cause is in question.
◦ Example: Inflation and unemployment are two economic phenomena studied extensively by economists.

• Spelling key: PHE + NOM + ENA. Note the sequence "nom" (as in "nominal") and the ending "-ena", not "-ina", "-omina" or "-ymena".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "phinomina" — incorrect; both vowel sounds "e" have been wrongly replaced with "i".

• Option 2: "fenomena" — incorrect; the initial sound is spelt with "f" instead of the correct "ph".

• Option 3: "phynamena" — incorrect; the middle syllable is wrongly spelt "nam" instead of "nom".

NOTE

• The singular form is "phenomenon"; the plural is "phenomena" — this is an irregular Greek-origin plural, similar to "criterion/criteria" and "datum/data".

• Other tricky "ph-" spelt words common in SSC exams: pharmacy, philosophy, phase, sphere, emphasis.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Serendipity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Misfortune.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Serendipity" means the occurrence of events by chance in a happy or beneficial way; good luck in making unexpected and fortunate discoveries. (सुखद संयोग/अनायास लाभ)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Misfortune", meaning bad luck; an unfortunate event or circumstance. (दुर्भाग्य)
◦ Example: Finding the rare manuscript was pure serendipity, quite unlike the series of misfortunes that had plagued his research earlier.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Tangibility" (स्पर्शनीयता) means the quality of being touchable or clearly real — the opposite of "intangibility", unrelated to luck.

• Option 3: "Permanency" (स्थायित्व) means the state of lasting indefinitely — the opposite of "temporariness", unrelated to luck.

• Option 4: "Tranquillity" (शांति) means the state of being calm and peaceful — the opposite of "turbulence" or "agitation", unrelated to luck.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Serendipity": fluke, windfall, providence, chance.

• The word was coined by writer Horace Walpole based on the Persian fairy tale "The Three Princes of Serendip", whose heroes made fortunate discoveries by accident.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Glad
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sad.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Glad" means feeling pleasure or happiness; delighted or pleased. (प्रसन्न/खुश)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Sad", meaning feeling or showing sorrow; unhappy. (दुखी)
◦ Example: She was glad to hear the good news, but her friend looked sad after failing the interview.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Jive" (बकवास/धोखा देना) as a noun/verb refers to a lively style of jazz music or dance, or informally to talk nonsense — unrelated to "glad".

• Option 2: "Innocent" (निर्दोष) means free from guilt or sin — the opposite of "guilty", not of "glad".

• Option 4: "Haunt" (सताना) means (of a ghost) to manifest itself at a place regularly, or to persistently trouble someone's mind — unrelated to "glad".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Glad": pleased, delighted, happy, content, cheerful.

• Other antonym pairs with "sad": sad ↔ glad, sad ↔ cheerful, sad ↔ joyful.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. It included a carbon tax on fossil fuels and incentives for businesses and individuals to adopt green practices.
B. The new policy aimed to reduce carbon emissions and promote renewable energy sources.
C. However, supporters of the policy argued that it was necessary to address the urgent threat of climate change and create a sustainable future for the planet.
D. The policy faced opposition from some industries and political groups who argued that it would hurt the economy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BADC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• To arrange jumbled sentences, identify the sentence that introduces the topic, then trace the logical flow of ideas — details, then contrast/opposition, then a counter-response — using linking words as clues.

• Sentence B — "The new policy aimed to reduce carbon emissions and promote renewable energy sources" — introduces the subject, "the new policy", for the first time, so it must be the opening sentence.

• Sentence A — "It included a carbon tax..." — uses the pronoun "It", which logically refers back to "the new policy" in B, and elaborates on what the policy contained. So A follows B.

• Sentence D — "The policy faced opposition..." — introduces a new development (opposition to the policy) after its features have been described in A, so D logically follows A.

• Sentence C — begins with "However", a contrast marker that directly opposes the opposition mentioned in D by presenting the supporters' viewpoint, so C must come last, after D.

• The coherent order is therefore: B → A → D → C.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "BCAD" is incorrect because it places the contrast sentence C ("However, supporters argued...") immediately after B, before the opposition in D is even mentioned — this makes the word "However" meaningless at that point.

• Option 3: "DABC" is incorrect because it opens with D ("The policy faced opposition..."), but "the policy" cannot be referred to before it has even been introduced in B.

• Option 4: "DACB" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3 — it begins with D, referring to "the policy" before it is introduced, and also disrupts the logical A→D→C flow.

NOTE

• Key clue words for para-jumbles: pronouns (it, they, this, these) usually refer back to a noun introduced in an earlier sentence; contrast markers (however, but, yet, on the other hand) signal a sentence that opposes the immediately preceding idea; and sentences with definite articles ("the policy") referring to something not yet named cannot open the paragraph.

• Always locate the opening sentence first (the one that introduces the subject in general terms, without pronouns referring backward) — this quickly eliminates wrong options.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined segment.
The music filled the room with a lot of happiness, expressing joyful melodies that brought smiles to everyone's faces.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. joy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Joy" means a feeling of great pleasure and happiness, which is precisely what "a lot of happiness" describes. (हर्ष/आनंद)
◦ Example: The music filled the room with joy, expressing joyful melodies that brought smiles to everyone's faces.

• The one-word substitute must convey the same intensity and type of positive emotion as the underlined phrase, and must also fit grammatically as a noun after the preposition "with".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "surprise" (आश्चर्य) means a feeling of mild astonishment caused by something unexpected — not the same as happiness.

• Option 3: "excitement" (उत्साह/उत्तेजना) refers to a feeling of great enthusiasm and eagerness, which is close but is not the precise synonym for "a lot of happiness" as clearly indicated by the context "joyful melodies" and "smiles".

• Option 4: "fear" (डर) means an unpleasant emotion caused by the threat of danger — the opposite of what is described in the sentence.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Joy": delight, happiness, gladness, bliss, elation.

• Watch for context clues like "joyful melodies" and "smiles" in comprehension-style vocabulary questions — they confirm the exact shade of meaning required, ruling out near-synonyms like "excitement".

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in active voice.
A play is being staged by our group this evening.
option_1: A play staged our group this evening.
option_2: Our group stages a play this evening.
option_3: Our group is staging a play this evening.
option_4: Our group staged a play this evening.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Our group is staging a play this evening.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "A play is being staged by our group this evening" is in the Passive Voice, Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "our group" becomes the subject; since it is treated as a singular collective subject, the auxiliary "is" is used; the verb "staged" (V3) becomes "staging" (V-ing); and "a play" becomes the object.

• Active form: Our group is staging a play this evening.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it omits the auxiliary verb entirely and uses the plain past form "staged", which does not correspond to any valid tense structure here.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "stages" is the Simple Present form, which does not match the Present Continuous sense ("is being staged") of the original passive sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "staged" is the Simple Past form, which does not match the Present Continuous ("is being staged") of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Time expressions like "this evening", "now", "at the moment", "currently" are strong indicators of the Continuous tense — always check them to confirm which tense (Simple vs. Continuous vs. Perfect) is being used.

• The passive of a Continuous tense always uses "being + V3"; the corresponding active always uses "V-ing".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Grave
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Frivolous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Grave", when used as an adjective, means serious or solemn, giving cause for alarm; important and requiring urgent attention. (गंभीर)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Frivolous", meaning not having any serious purpose or value; carefree and silly. (तुच्छ/छिछोरा)
◦ Example: The board treated the data breach as a grave matter, not a frivolous complaint to be dismissed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Native" (मूल निवासी) means belonging to a particular place by birth — unrelated in meaning to "grave".

• Option 3: "Foreign" (विदेशी) is the antonym of "native", not of "grave".

• Option 4: "Serious" (गंभीर) is actually a synonym of "grave" in this sense, not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Grave" (adjective): serious, solemn, severe, critical, weighty.

• Note that "grave" is also a noun meaning a burial place — context determines which sense (and hence which antonym) is intended; here the adjective sense is clearly used, as confirmed by the option "Serious" being offered as a distractor synonym.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The constitutional right to vote
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Franchise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Franchise" means the constitutional or legal right to vote in public elections. (मताधिकार)
◦ Example: Universal adult franchise ensures that every eligible citizen has the constitutional right to vote.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Polling" (मतदान की प्रक्रिया) refers to the process or act of voting/recording votes, not the legal right itself.

• Option 3: "Voting" (मतदान) refers to the act of casting a vote, not the constitutional right that entitles someone to do so.

• Option 4: "Buttoning" means fastening with buttons — entirely unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• "Franchise" also has another common meaning in business — an authorization granted to a person/group to market a company's goods or services in a particular area; context determines which sense applies.

• Related one-word substitutions: "Suffrage" is a close synonym of "franchise" in the sense of the right to vote, and "Disenfranchise" means to deprive someone of this right.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the given situation.
Aurangzeb, the famous Mughal ruler, found that he had caught someone more powerful than him in the form of the brave Maratha, Shivaji.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Catching a tartar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To catch a Tartar" means to deal with or confront a person or situation that turns out to be far more powerful, troublesome, or difficult to handle than expected. (अपने से अधिक शक्तिशाली व्यक्ति से पाला पड़ना)
◦ Example: The bully picked a fight with the new boy, not realising he had caught a Tartar — the boy was a trained boxer.

• In the given situation, Aurangzeb expected to easily overpower Shivaji but instead found him to be a much stronger and more capable adversary than anticipated — a perfect match for this idiom.

• The idiom is said to derive from a soldier who reported "catching" a Tartar (a fierce Central Asian warrior) but, on being asked to bring the prisoner in, replied that the Tartar would not let him go — he had, in effect, been caught himself.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Nipping in the bud" (शुरुआत में ही रोक देना): to stop something at an early stage before it can develop further — not relevant to facing a stronger opponent.

• Option 2: "Changing the hands" (मालिकाना हक बदलना): used to describe ownership or control passing from one person/group to another — not relevant here.

• Option 4: "Blazing the trail" (नया मार्ग प्रशस्त करना): to be the first to do something, pioneering a new path for others to follow — not relevant to this situation.

NOTE

• Other idioms describing encounters with unexpectedly strong opponents/situations: "To bite off more than one can chew" (to take on more than one can manage), "To meet one's match" (to encounter someone equally or more capable than oneself).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
I don't think he can dance as wellest Elena.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. as well as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence compares two people's ability to dance and expresses equality between them at the positive degree, not a difference of degree.

• Rule — Comparison of Equality: to compare two things/persons at the same level, the structure "as + adjective/adverb (positive degree) + as" is used — never the comparative ("-er than") or superlative ("-est") form.

• "Well" is an adverb whose comparative is "better" and superlative is "best"; there is no such word as "wellest" or "weller" in Standard English.

• Applying the equality-comparison rule to the positive degree adverb "well": "as well as".

• Corrected sentence: "I don't think he can dance as well as Elena."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "weller than" is incorrect because "weller" is not a valid comparative form of "well" (the correct comparative is "better"), and "than" is used for comparisons of inequality/degree, not the sense intended here.

• Option 2: "wellest" is incorrect because "wellest" is not a valid superlative form of "well" (the correct superlative is "best").

• Option 4: "well than" is incorrect because "than" must follow a comparative form (e.g. "better than"), and pairing it directly with the positive degree "well" is ungrammatical.

NOTE

• Irregular degrees of comparison: well → better → best; good → better → best; bad → worse → worst; little → less → least; much/many → more → most.

• The equality structure "as...as" always takes the positive degree of the adjective/adverb, e.g. "as tall as", "as quickly as", "as good as" — never the comparative or superlative form.

question:
Comprehension:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

Such examples of commercial success, of innovation, drive, vision, determination, adaptability, and adventure are anchored in the basic Indian openness to, and talent for, acquiring material wealth. For every success story there are, of course, dozens of failures. Traditional Indian firms have their strengths, but also their weaknesses, and of these perhaps the most debilitating are a lack of team work and a weakness for quick profit. These reflect ingrained ways of thinking and planning, as does the distrust of anyone outside the family, which inhibits the adoption of modern practices of management. But such weaknesses are more than compensated for by the desire to succeed, which is probably more intense in India, given the omnipresent fear of poverty, the cut-throat competition for each opportunity, and the asphyxiating hold of hierarchy.

What has the Indian talent for acquiring material wealth led to?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Commercial success, innovation, adaptability.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage opens with the line: "Such examples of commercial success, of innovation, drive, vision, determination, adaptability, and adventure are anchored in the basic Indian openness to, and talent for, acquiring material wealth."

• This directly states that the Indian talent for acquiring material wealth has led to (is the basis/anchor of) qualities and outcomes such as commercial success, innovation, and adaptability, among others listed in the sentence.

• Reading-comprehension rule: for a direct factual question, the correct option must be the one whose wording is explicitly supported by the passage, without contradicting or adding information not stated in the text.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Commercial success, stagnation, innovation" is incorrect because the passage nowhere mentions "stagnation" — in fact the passage describes dynamism (success, drive, adventure), the opposite of stagnation.

• Option 2: "Adaptability, quick profit, opportunity" is incorrect because "a weakness for quick profit" is listed in the passage as a weakness of traditional Indian firms, not as an outcome of the talent for acquiring wealth.

• Option 4: "Determination, team work, adventure" is incorrect because, although "determination" and "adventure" are mentioned, "team work" is explicitly described in the passage as something Indian firms lack ("a lack of team work"), not as an outcome of the talent for wealth.

NOTE

• In factual RC questions, always match the option against the exact wording of the passage — options that mix in a plausible-sounding but textually unsupported or contradictory word (like "stagnation" or "team work" here) are common distractors called "partially true" options.

• Always re-read the specific sentence being tested rather than relying on a general impression of the whole passage, since SSC RC distractors are often built by subtly swapping one word for its opposite or an unrelated term.

What are the weaknesses of traditional Indian firms?
option_1: Ingrained ways of thinking and adoption of modern practices of management
option_2: A weakness for quick profit and the openness to acquiring wealth
option_3: A lack of team work and the cut-throat competition
option_4: A lack of team work and a weakness for quick profit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A lack of team work and a weakness for quick profit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states: "Traditional Indian firms have their strengths, but also their weaknesses, and of these perhaps the most debilitating are a lack of team work and a weakness for quick profit."

• This sentence explicitly and directly names the two weaknesses of traditional Indian firms as a lack of team work and a weakness for quick profit — matching Option 4 exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Ingrained ways of thinking and adoption of modern practices of management" is incorrect because the passage says these ingrained ways of thinking "inhibit" (prevent) the adoption of modern management practices — adoption of modern practices is not itself described as a weakness; rather, the lack of such adoption is implied to be the problem.

• Option 2: "A weakness for quick profit and the openness to acquiring wealth" is incorrect because "openness to...acquiring material wealth" is described in the passage as the basic strength/talent behind commercial success, not a weakness.

• Option 3: "A lack of team work and the cut-throat competition" is incorrect because "cut-throat competition" is mentioned later in the passage as a reason the desire to succeed is intense — it is not listed as a weakness of firms.

NOTE

• When passage sentences list two paired items directly (e.g. "X and Y are the weaknesses"), the correct answer will reproduce both items precisely — an option that swaps in even one unrelated (though passage-mentioned) term is a distractor.

• Distinguish carefully between what the passage calls a strength/cause (e.g. openness to wealth, desire to succeed) versus a weakness/effect (lack of team work, weakness for quick profit) — RC distractors often deliberately mix the two categories.

Why is the desire to succeed more intense in India?
option_1: Due to the hold of hierarchy, fear of poverty, and a lack of team work
option_2: Due to fear of poverty, a lack of team work and distrust of the outsider
option_3: Due to cut-throat competition, distrust of the outsider and fear of poverty
option_4: Due to fear of poverty, cut-throat competition, and the hold of hierarchy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Due to fear of poverty, cut-throat competition, and the hold of hierarchy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states: "...such weaknesses are more than compensated for by the desire to succeed, which is probably more intense in India, given the omnipresent fear of poverty, the cut-throat competition for each opportunity, and the asphyxiating hold of hierarchy."

• This sentence directly lists the three reasons the desire to succeed is more intense in India: the fear of poverty, the cut-throat competition, and the hold of hierarchy — matching Option 4 exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Due to the hold of hierarchy, fear of poverty, and a lack of team work" is incorrect because "a lack of team work" is listed elsewhere in the passage as a weakness of firms, not as a reason for the intense desire to succeed.

• Option 2: "Due to fear of poverty, a lack of team work and distrust of the outsider" is incorrect because both "a lack of team work" and "distrust of anyone outside the family" belong to the passage's discussion of firms' weaknesses, not to the reasons for the intense desire to succeed.

• Option 3: "Due to cut-throat competition, distrust of the outsider and fear of poverty" is incorrect because "distrust of the outsider" is again drawn from the weaknesses discussion, not the sentence about the desire to succeed.

NOTE

• This question tests the ability to locate the exact supporting sentence in a passage with several similarly-themed lists (weaknesses vs. reasons for the desire to succeed) — always trace each option's components back to the specific sentence that answers the specific question asked.

• A common RC trap is combining two true-but-mismatched facts from different parts of the passage into a single, plausible-sounding but incorrect option.

Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word with reference to its usage in the passage.
Debilitating
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Invigorating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the passage, "debilitating" is used in the phrase "the most debilitating [weaknesses]", meaning weakening; making someone or something weak or feeble. (कमजोर करने वाला)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Invigorating", meaning making one feel strong, healthy, and full of energy; strengthening. (शक्ति देने वाला/स्फूर्तिदायक)
◦ Example: While the constant losses were debilitating for the firm's morale, the new leadership brought an invigorating sense of purpose.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Enfeebling" (दुर्बल करने वाला) is a synonym of "debilitating" — it also means making weak.

• Option 2: "Crippling" (अपंग करने वाला/भारी क्षति पहुंचाने वाला) is also a synonym of "debilitating" — it means severely damaging or disabling.

• Option 4: "Undermining" (कमजोर करना/क्षति पहुंचाना) is likewise a synonym of "debilitating" — it means weakening or damaging something gradually.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Debilitating": weakening, enfeebling, crippling, sapping, undermining.

• When a question asks for the antonym of a word "with reference to its usage in the passage", always re-check the exact sentence, since some words are polysemous (have multiple meanings) and only the passage-specific sense should be used to find the antonym.

These reflect ingrained ways of thinking and planning, as does the distrust of anyone outside the family, which inhibits the adoption of modern practices of management. But such weaknesses are more than compensated for by the desire to succeed, which is probably more intense in India, given the omnipresent fear of poverty, the cut-throat competition for each opportunity, and the asphyxiating hold of hierarchy.

Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word with reference to its usage in the passage.
Asphyxiating
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Smothering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the passage, "asphyxiating" is used in the phrase "the asphyxiating hold of hierarchy", meaning suffocating; stifling; depriving of the ability to breathe or function freely. (दम घोंटने वाला)

• Its most appropriate synonym is "Smothering", meaning suppressing or stifling something completely, as if depriving it of air. (दबाने वाला/घुटन भरा)
◦ Example: Employees often complained about the asphyxiating, smothering hold of hierarchy that stifled any new idea before it could be discussed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Emancipating" (मुक्त करने वाला) means setting free from restriction — the opposite of "asphyxiating".

• Option 2: "Liberating" (स्वतंत्र करने वाला) means giving freedom — again the opposite of "asphyxiating".

• Option 4: "Unfettering" (बंधनमुक्त करना) means removing restraints or shackles — also the opposite of "asphyxiating".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Asphyxiating": suffocating, stifling, smothering, choking.

• Note the pattern in this question set: three of the four options (Emancipating, Liberating, Unfettering) are all synonyms of one another and antonyms of the keyword — a common SSC technique to test whether the candidate has correctly understood the word's actual (negative) sense rather than confusing it with a positive one.
